manuscript.title: A cost-efficient IoT service placement approach using whale optimization algorithm in fog computing environment
manuscript.abstract_text: The rapid development of Internet of Things (IoT)-based applications and the era of 5G networks has led to an exponential increase in the amount of data required for processing the IoT services. The fog computing paradigm has emerged as a distributed computing solution for serving these applications using available fog nodes near the IoT devices. Since the IoT applications are developed in the form of several IoT services with various quality of service (QoS) requirements that can be deployed on the fog nodes with different resource capabilities in the fog ecosystem, finding an efficient service placement plan is one of the challenging issues to be considered. In this paper, we propose an efficient IoT service placement solution based on the autonomic methodology for deploying IoT applications on the fog infrastructure. Our proposed solution monitors the QoS requirements of IoT services and capabilities of available fog nodes to determine an efficient service placement plan using the whale opti- mization algorithm (WOA) meta-heuristic technique. Besides, our evolutionary-based mechanism utilized the throughput and the energy consumption as objective functions for finding desirable IoT service placement plan while meeting the QoS requirements of each IoT service. Also, we develop an autonomous service placement framework according to a three-tier architecture of the fog ecosystem to show the interaction between the main components of the IoT device and fog layers for deploying IoT applications. The simulation results demonstrate that the proposed solution increases the resource usage and service acceptance ratio and reduces the service delay and the energy consumption compared with the other metaheuristic-based mechanisms.

sections.body_text: In recent years, the fog computing paradigm emerged as a distrib- uted computing paradigm to provide storage, computing, and networking capabilities for serving the Internet of Things (IoT) appli- cations at the edge of the network (Atlam, Walters, & Wills, 2018, Brogi, Forti, Guerrero, & Lera, 2019). Fog computing technology deploys IoT applications on the available fog resources to minimize cost, latency, bandwidth usage, and satisfy the quality of service (QoS) requirements for real-time applications such as virtual reality, autonomous cars, augmented reality, real-time manufacturing, drones, and cyber-physical system in IoT networks (Yousefpour et al., 2019). According to micro- service architecture, the IoT applications are developed in the form of several IoT services that are loosely coupled with various QoS re- quirements that can deploy in different locations. On the other hand, in the fog ecosystem, the fog layer consists of a network of resource-limited fog nodes with different resource capabilities. The IoT service placement problem is deploying IoT services on the fog nodes with different resource capabilities while satisfying various QoS requirements of IoT services (Omer Hassan, Azizi, & Shojafar, 2020). It has a considerable impact on the performance and energy consumption of fog resources in the fog ecosystem. Some IoT applications are delay-sensitive, such as virtual reality and online gaming, while others are compute-intensive, such as big data analytics applications. On the other hand, due to the heterogeneity and resource-limited fog nodes and various requirements of IoT applications, providing an effective placement plan is one of the most challenging tasks that should be considered. Evolutionary algo- rithms are a subset of optimization techniques inspired by natural evo- lution operators such as mutation, selection, and crossover within specific constraints to solve service placement problems. Since the ser- vice placement problem is known as an NP-hard optimization problem, the evolutionary algorithms such as genetic algorithm (GA) (Skarlat, Nardelli, Schulte, Borkowski, & Leitner, 2017, Guerrero, Lera, & Juiz, 2019a, Canali & Lancellotti, 2019), particle swarm optimization (PSO) (Djemai, Stolf, Monteil, & Pierson, 2019, Roy et al., 2020), and Simu- lated Annealing (SA) (Santoyo-Gonz´alez & Cervell´o-Pastor, 2018) are

In this section, we will review the application placement mechanisms in the fog/edge computing environment. Then, we summarize different works to solve the application placement problem. Skarlat et al. (Skarlat et al., 2017) have presented a service placement solution using a genetic algorithm in a fog computing network. Their solution considers the application QoS requirements and the fog resources heterogeneity to achieve a suitable placement plan. Besides, they described a conceptual hierarchical framework by intro­ ducing fog orchestration nodes to manage several fog colonies. Their obtained results demonstrated that their proposed solution improves in terms of fog resources utilization and IoT service execution time compared with other approaches. Guerrero et al. (Guerrero et al., 2019) have studied the suitability of various metaheuristic-based techniques for the IoT service placemen in the fog computing environment. Their study adapted three evolutionary algorithms to the specific scope by defining a set of evolutionary operators and optimizing evolutionary algorithms. Besides, they formalized three objective functions: minimi­ zation of latency, resource usage, and service spread. Their results illustrated that the NSGA-II algorithm is superior to other evolutionary algorithms in terms of mentioned objective functions. Canali et al. (Canali & Lancellotti, 2019) have proposed an optimization solution for allocating data sensor workload on fog devices. Their solution considers the processing time and communication latency between IoT devices and fog devices. Also, they presented a heuristic-based mechanism using a genetic algorithm to achieve a scalable solution for large-scale service placement issues. They evaluated their solution on the smart city application and demonstrated that they achieve the best solution than other evolutionary algorithms. Djemai et al. (Djemai et al., 2019) have proposed an IoT service placement approach using discrete particle swarm optimization, which considers service delay for minimizing en­ ergy consumption. Their approach considers various logical topologies for IoT applications with service delay requirements to achieve a delay- energy trade-off. According to their simulation results, their proposed approach prefers the fog layer, then depending on the IoT application, it selects between the IoT device and cloud layer. Roy et al. (Roy et al., 2020) have studied the multimedia service placement problem in the mobile edge computing network. They formulated their problem as a linear programming formulation and utilized particle swarm optimization as a meta-heuristic mechanism to solve their problem within polynomial time. Gonz´alez et al. (Santoyo- Gonz´alez & Cervell´o-Pastor, 2018) have proposed a latency-aware strategy for fog service placement under 5G mobile network. They mathematically formulated the fog service placement problem in the form of a mixed-integer linear programming model. They presented a hybrid heuristic-based mechanism using simulated annealing according to the traffic generator’s place to solve the formulated problem. Finally, they developed a desktop application to obtain the flexibility and us­ ability of the proposed strategy. In (Guerrero, Lera, & Juiz, 2019b), a decentralized mechanism has been proposed to solve service placement problems in a fog computing environment. Their mechanism considers usage data and performance obtained in each fog node, and it is locally performed in each fog node to migrate micro-services to upper fog nodes. Besides, their mechanism considers the interoperability and migration between the micro-services. They validated their mechanism using the iFogSim toolkit by modelling microservice-based applications and indicated that their solution improves service latency and network usage compared with other mechanisms. Lin et al. (Lin, Deng, Suwatcharachaitiwong, & Li, 2020) have proposed a bat-inspired algo­ rithm to solve IoT service placement in the fog landscape. Their pro­ posed solution simulates the food-searching behaviour of bats for deploying weighted fog devices to achieve a better solution than the PSO-based approach. Forti et al. (Forti, Ferrari, & Brogi, 2020) have developed a methodology using declarative programming called SecFog for mapping IoT services with various security requirements on fog devices with different security capabilities. Their methodology con­ siders the trust model among various stakeholders by managing fog infrastructures to determine the most secure service deployments using reducing manual tuning. They prototyped their methodology using ProbLog language for deploying IoT services to achieve appropriate trade-offs between the required security level and energy consumption.

The complexity of the administrative activities of the computer systems and their integration with heterogeneous systems as the main motivations for autonomous computer systems are considered. In 2001, IBM introduced the autonomic computing paradigm to describe a computer system that is able to adjust to environmental changes with minimal user intervention (Lalanda, McCann, & Diaconescu, 2013). Autonomic computing provides computer systems with self- management features to manage themselves, autonomously.

In this section, we explain an autonomic-based IoT service placement approach in more detail. We first develop an autonomous service placement framework for deploying IoT applications into the three-tier fog landscape. Then, we provide a formulation for the IoT service placement problem. Finally, an efficient service placement algorithm using the WOA technique to deploy the IoT services is described.

In this section, an autonomous framework for deploying IoT services on the virtual fog infrastructure to fulfil the proposed solution will be described, as shown in Fig. 4. The proposed framework includes three layers: the thing layer, the fog layer, and the cloud layer. The thing layer as the bottom layer consists of a series of smart objects such as tablets and mobile phones to gather the required information from the fog landscape. The fog layer as the main layer is located between the thing and cloud layers and includes a set of slave fog domains to handle the IoT user requests in different geo-distributed locations. Each fog domain consists of several fog nodes with different resource capabilities to serve IoT services according to their QoS requirements and a domain control node. The master fog domain is responsible for determining the strategy of the dispatch and deployment of the IoT services among the fog do­ domains in certain Δt time intervals according to the autonomic computing model. It keeps the collected information about fog nodes through the control nodes of each slave fog domain into the shared knowledge base.

According to their deadline parameter, it verifies IoT services to send the delay-sensitive services to the master fog domain for deploying on the fog infrastructure and other IoT services through cloud gateway to the cloud layer are transferred, as shown in Fig. 5. We consider several fog domains in the fog ecosystem which together cooperate in a master/slave manner. The fog domains are micro-data centres that include a set of fog nodes and a fog domain control node. Each fog node as a computational resource provides the processing power, memory, and storage capabilities for deploying and serving the IoT services. The fog domain control node is a powerful fog node in Fig. 4. The proposed framework.

The master fog domain as the most important component in the fog landscape is responsible for managing and deploying the IoT services received from the admission control component in an autonomic fashion. It keeps the required information about the QoS requirements of IoT services and capabilities of available fog nodes into its knowledge base. Therefore, it utilized the MAPE-k loop to dispatch IoT services between the suitable slave fog domains. The master fog domain acts according to four sub-components: monitor, analyzer, planner, and executor. The monitor sub-component gathers the required information about the capabilities of available fog nodes and QoS requirements of IoT services and stores them into the shared database to use by others. The analyzer sub-component prioritizes IoT services using the infor­ mation collected (i.e., deadline and waiting time) by the monitor. Then, the planner component as the core of the master fog domain determines an appropriate placement plan using the WOA technique and then saves it into the knowledge base to be used by the executor sub-component. Finally, the determined placement solution is performed by the exec­ tor. These sub-components regularly cooperated at given time intervals to deploy the IoT services on the suitable fog nodes according to their QoS requirements.

The main components in the cloud layer are cloud servers and cloud gateway. The cloud servers provide the storage and processing capa­ bilities to serve IoT applications based on the pay-per-use model. The cloud servers serve compute-intensive or data-intensive IoT applica­ tions, which require heavy compute processing and storage capabilities in a long time interval. In this section, we present an efficient IoT service placement algo­ rithm (i.e., Algorithm1) based on an autonomic computing model named MAPE-k loop for deploying IoT applications in a fog ecosystem. The fog control node within the master fog domain periodically executes and repeats the proposed algorithm according to monitoring, analysis, planning, and execution phases at given time intervals, regularly (lines 2–7). Initially, the IoT services received through admission control and the available fog nodes are monitored by the monitoring phase, and the required information is stored in the knowledge base (line 3). Then, the analysis phase refines and examines this recorded information to pri­ oritize IoT applications for deploying on the fog infrastructure. Indeed, it acts as a pre-processing task for the planning phase (line 3). Afterwards, the planning phase utilized the WOA technique to find an efficient ser­ vice placement plan for deploying IoT applications on the fog nodes (line 5). Finally, the execution phase performs the placement plan obtained from the previous phase to meet various QoS requirements of IoT ap­ plications (line 6).

Indeed, this phase determines that the IoT service requested be deployed on which fog domain and which fog node controlled under that fog domain. The time complexity of the proposed algorithm depends on the required time for generating the initial population, calculating the fitness function, and the main body of the proposed algorithm including the exploration and exploration phases. The time complexity of gener­ ating the initial population (lines 2–8) depends on the population size (i. e., N) and the size of each candidate solution (i.e., J), and it is equal toO(J × N). The computational complexity of the fitness function (i. e.,O(fitness)) to calculate the value of candidate solutions and it is specified by the application which depends on the number of IoT service and the number of fog nodes. Since solutions are illustrated with a matrix W of the size |L| × |J| where |L| is the number of IoT services and |J| is the number of fog nodes. Therefore, the computational complexity of the fitness function can be specified asO(fitness) = O(L × J). Also, the time complexity of the main loop (lines 11–28) depends on the maximum number of iteration, the population size, and the size of each candidate solution and it is expressed byO(Maxt × N × (J + O(fitness))). Since N, Maxt and O(fitness) are linear with respect to n, the total time complexity of the proposed algorithm can be described asO(J × N) + O(Maxt × N × (J + O(fitness))) ≅O(n3). Therefore, the WOA-FSP algo­ rithm is an approximation solution with polynomial time complexity.

In this section, we provide the simulation setting to develop exper­ iments for validating the effectiveness of the proposed approach in more detail. To model and simulate the fog ecosystem and IoT services, we utilize the iFogSim toolkit (Gupta, Vahid Dastjerdi, Ghosh, & Buyya, 2017) with some modifications of the classes to characterize the fog infrastructure, IoT applications, and resource management algorithms. It provided a series of classes for modelling fog infrastructure (e.g., Sensor, Actuator, and Fog. Device classes) and IoT applications (e.g., AppEdge, AppModule, and AppLoop classes). In this study, we use three main class categories, namely: physical, logical, and control to simulate and validate our proposed service placement solution in the iFogSim library. The physical entities include IoT sensors, gateways, fog devices, cloud servers, links, and they have been implemented by the classes of FogDevice, Sensor, Actuator, and Tuple. The FogDevice class is one of the most important classes of the iFogSim library to model fog nodes, and it is expressed by its resource attributes include the power processing, the main memory, and the disk capacities, and the network bandwidth. The Sensor class is utilized to model the IoT devices into the IoT layer to generate tuples according to Table 3. The Actuator class has utilized the tuples of fog devices to determine and perform the placement plan. The Tuple is a class to simulate the data flow among the entities according to the triggered events in the fog environment, and it is characterized by at­ tributes include the source, destination, and type. The logical entities include the IoT applications that are modelled as a series of modules with their attributes, and they have been stimulated by the classes of AppModule, AppEdge, and AppLoop. The AppModule and the AppEdge classes are utilized to model the IoT services and the relationship between them, respectively. Besides, the AppLoop class is used to determine a set of the IoT services according to the user’s favorite workflow starting from the beginning of the loop to the IoT service where the loop finishes. The control entities include two classes of Controller and ModuleMapping for placing the IoT applications on the fog nodes. We use the ModuleMapping class to implement the WOA-FSP al­ gorithm to find an efficient placement plan. The Controller class launches the IoT applications on the fog resources according to the placement plan and then it gathers the performance metrics such as service delay, energy consumption, and resource usage during the simulation process. Also, we performed the simulation experiments on a personal com­ puter with Intel Core i7 2.4 GHz CPU, 1 TB disk, and 8 GB of RAM running Windows 10-64bit. Besides, we used the random uniform dis­ tribution to generate the synthetic dataset for simulation experiments. Therefore, we set the properties of resource demands for IoT services and fog resource capabilities, according to Tables 4 and 5, respectively.

One of the proposed cost-efficient IoT service placement algorithm applications is robotic assistance, which is an essential aspect of Industry 4.0. For example, various surveillance equipment, including IP and analogue cameras, are installed in smart factories. Industrial robots analyze the taken photos by these cameras and then extract features for taking appropriate emergency decisions (M. Afrin, Jin, Rahman, Tian, & Kulkarni, 2019). On the one hand, image quality can be affected by weather, lighting condition, or being in an outdoor or an indoor posi­ tion. On the other hand, the utilized equipment for capturing the image could be in a different technology or brand. These conditions lead to images with different qualities that may suffer from loss of information. As a result, many image processing techniques and their services should be considered to enhance the quality of the images and recover the lost information. Image Enhancement methods for colour image enhance­ ment include Homomorphic Filtering, Contrast Stretching, Retinex, Wavelet Multiscale Transform, and Histogram Equalization (Vishwa­ karma & Mishra, 2012). Fog nodes are responsible for processing the received images from the robots. Then the proposed service placement algorithm monitors the requirements of the requested services and the capabilities of available fog nodes to determine an efficient service placement strategy. Finally, the improved and recovered images are sent back to the robots for further analysis and emergency decision making.
